If you never dive under the hood on your Linux system, it shouldn't matter either way.

If you do (or if you don't but someone you consider "friend" does and will do that for you), then avoid systemd like the plague. Sure, there are some things that systemd appears to make easier, but there are plenty more things (as indicated in that link) that it makes very poor decisions on.

Myself, I have made the decision to move away from distros that utilize systemd. Even when one chooses to use another init system, systemd is still there in the background, because those distros have chosen to depend so heavily on it.

In my opinion, it's best to settle on a distro that never had systemd to begin with, like Slackware, SalixOS, or any of a handful of others. Devuan is making great strides to getting there, if they're not there already.

Avoid Debian, Ubuntu, Red Hat/Fedora/CentOS, if your goal is to avoid systemd.

The main problem with SystemD that a lot of people have it that it is one program that is handling multiple things. This can lead to software bloat which will eventually slow down performance. But right now, systemd is doing pretty good.

Systemd was developed to replace older, not as well performing software, and once we get to the point that systemd is depreciated, something else will be forked to created from scratch that will replace it. So it is not something that you need to worry about unless you are actively developing linux distros.
